rules.statement: Put an optional capability in its own opt-in package that depends only on the general slice's abstractions, and never make a general package (or its implementation) reference that capability's packages.
rules.why: Coupling a general slice to one optional capability forces every host to carry it whether or not it wants it, and leaks the capability's shapes into the general abstractions.
rules.check: Look for a project reference or using from a general/base package to an optional capability's package, or a capability package referencing the base implementation package instead of its abstractions.

rules.statement: Don't add a capability-specific method to a shared base abstraction (such as an audit recorder); expose one generic entry point that takes a caller-supplied event subtype, and let each capability own its event type and a convenience extension method.
rules.why: A per-capability method puts a capability's shape on a general abstraction; one generic entry point serves every capability.
rules.check: Look for new methods on a shared interface or base class named after one specific feature or resource type, or event types/resource-type constants for a capability declared in the base package.

rules.statement: Don't make an opt-in library check at runtime whether it is itself registered (for example returning 501 when a feature is missing); treat registration as presence and enforce prerequisites at compile time by having the registration extension take the prerequisite's service builder as a required parameter.
rules.why: Self-detection is meaningless once the feature is an opt-in package, and a required builder parameter turns a missing prerequisite into a compile error instead of a startup or resolution failure.
rules.check: Look for endpoints or services that probe the container for their own registration or return 501 Not Implemented, and for Add* extensions whose required dependency is only resolved at runtime rather than demanded as a parameter.

rules.statement: When a capability package needs base-class plumbing that lives in another package's implementation, make it a public base type in that package's abstractions and derive from it, rather than copying the plumbing into the capability package.
rules.why: Duplicated endpoint plumbing (authorization, paging, error mapping, serialization) drifts from the original.
rules.check: Look for a new package that reimplements helpers or a base handler already present internally elsewhere, instead of deriving from a public abstraction.

rules.statement: Authorize every end-user account management operation against the tenant scope resource, and don't model end-user accounts as ownable resources with an owners sub-resource.
rules.why: Authority over an end-user subject is tenant administration, so an owner model adds a resource type and sub-resource for no authority a tenant administrator lacks.
rules.check: Look for account management handlers that authorize against an account-level or ownable resource rather than the tenant scope, or that add owner endpoints for accounts.

rules.statement: When creating a local account, write the account, its principal and its self-issued identity in one unit of work rather than creating the principal lazily on first login or first metadata write.
rules.why: Metadata and authority need a principal as target from the moment the account exists, and lazy creation scatters provisioning across read paths and leaves a window with no principal.
rules.check: Look for account create paths that don't create the principal and identity in the same transaction, or metadata/login paths that materialize a missing principal.

rules.statement: Allow server-trusted (system) subject metadata to be written only through administrator-gated paths such as account create and the administrator metadata endpoint, never through an end-user-reachable path or folded into a general account update.
rules.why: System metadata carries the owner-versus-server trust boundary and must never be writable by an end user.
rules.check: Look for new write paths to system metadata, especially ones reachable by end users or added to a general account update operation.

rules.statement: When deleting an end-user account, end the principal's sessions before removing it (and remove the principal when it was its last identity); when disabling an account or resetting its password, end its sessions after the commit.
rules.why: A disabled, deleted or reset end user must lose its existing sessions.
rules.check: Look for delete, disable or password-reset handlers that don't revoke sessions, or that revoke them in the wrong order relative to the commit.

rules.statement: Judge every password that is set (account create, password reset) with the single password policy service and answer a refusal with a 400 problem response.
rules.why: A password is judged by one policy wherever it is set.
rules.check: Look for password-setting code paths that skip the password policy, apply their own checks, or return a status other than a 400 problem on refusal.
